title: Why this JavaScript loop prints 3, 3, 3
description:
A classic JavaScript gotcha: a loop that looks like it counts 0, 1, 2 actually logs 3, 3, 3. The reason is that var is function-scoped, so every callback closes over the same single variable. Swap in let and each iteration gets a fresh binding. This is the heart of how closures work -- they capture variables, not values.

Source lesson(s):
- https://sigilipelli.github.io/javascript-mastery-path/level-2/01-closures-scope/

#Shorts

beats.narration: Here's a classic JavaScript trick question. This loop counts from zero to two and schedules three callbacks. You'd expect zero, one, two. It actually prints three, three, three.
The reason is that var isn't block scoped. There's only ever one i for the whole loop. By the time the callbacks run, the loop has finished and i is three for every one of them.
Swap var for let and it just works. let creates a fresh binding on every iteration, so each callback closes over its own copy of the counter.

display.output:
let j: 0
let j: 1
let j: 2

beats.narration: That's the key to closures. They capture variables, not values. A function remembers the scope it was born in, and it sees that variable live, not a snapshot.
